marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q019.takeaway: Free-water clearance reflects urine dilution or concentration and is regulated chiefly by ADH-mediated collecting-duct water permeability.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q019.displayText:
Free-water clearance reflects urine dilution or concentration and is regulated chiefly by ADH-mediated collecting-duct water permeability.

Free water clearance is regulated by ADH.
Free water clearance is defined as the amount of solute-free water generated by the kidneys, either
when dilute urine or when concentrated urine is formed.
Free-water clearance is positive, when excess water is being excreted (dilute urine).
Free-water clearance is negative, when excess solutes are being removed and water is being
conserved (concentrated urine).
emphasis: Free-water clearance reflects urine dilution or concentration and is regulated chiefly by ADH-mediated collecting-duct water permeability

rationales.b: Aldosterone regulates distal sodium and potassium transport, not the principal free-water handling signal.
rationales.c: Loop diuretics disrupt the medullary gradient and can alter free-water handling.
rationales.d: ADH is a major regulator, so the “none” choice is false.

Solution to Question’23:
The requirements for excreting concentrated urine are high ADH levels and hyperosmolar renal
medulla.
A high level of ADH, which increases the permeability of the distal tubules and collecting ducts to
water, thereby allowing these tubular segments to avidly reabsorb water, and a high osmolarity of
the renal medullary interstitial fluid, which provides the osmotic gradient necessary for water
reabsorption to occur in the presence of high levels of ADH.

Solution to Question 24:
Maximum osmotic gradient is found in the inner medulla. The gradient of osmolarity from the
cortex (300 mosm/L) to the inner medulla (1200 mosm/L) is produced by the loops of Henle as
countercurrent multipliers and maintained by operation of the vasa recta as countercurrent
exchangers.

Solution to Question 29:
Thin ascending limb is not a component of the countercurrent mechanism.
The loop of Henle function as countercurrent multipliers and vasa recta as countercurrent
exchangers.
The functioning of the loop of Henle depends upon:

¢ Active transport of Na+ and Cl- from the thick ascending limb
¢ Inflow of tubular fluid from proximal tubule and outflow to the distal tubule.

hence do contribute passively to countercurrent multiplication. However, among the options

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q023.takeaway: Concentrated urine requires both high ADH and a hyperosmotic renal medullary interstitium.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q023.displayText:
Concentrated urine requires both high ADH and a hyperosmotic renal medullary interstitium.

The requirements for excreting concentrated urine are high ADH levels and hyperosmolar renal medulla.
A high level of ADH, which increases the permeability of the distal tubules and collecting ducts to water, thereby allowing these tubular segments to avidly reabsorb water, and a high osmolarity of the renal medullary interstitial fluid, which provides the osmotic gradient necessary for water reabsorption to occur in the presence of high levels of ADH.
emphasis: Concentrated urine requires both high ADH and a hyperosmotic renal medullary interstitium

rationales.a: A hypo-osmotic medulla cannot draw water out of collecting ducts even with high ADH.
rationales.b: Low ADH leaves collecting ducts relatively water-impermeable.
rationales.d: A high medullary gradient without ADH cannot strongly increase collecting-duct water permeability.

emphasis: The thin ascending limb is relatively impermeable to water and passive NaCl reabsorption is not the classic driving component; its asserted sodium outflow is the exception

rationales.a: Thick ascending salt reabsorption is a principal driver of medullary countercurrent multiplication.
rationales.b: Water leaves the thin descending limb into the hyperosmotic medulla.
rationales.d: Tubular fluid flows through the nephron continuously, enabling countercurrent multiplication.

emphasis: Chloride concentration rises along the PCT as water and bicarbonate are reabsorbed; amino acids, glucose and bicarbonate concentrations decline

rationales.d: Bicarbonate is reclaimed in the PCT, lowering its tubular concentration.
